title: The Table of Nations
intro: Genesis 10 lists the descendants of Noah's three sons. Jewish tradition counts seventy nations here: Japheth 14, Ham 30, Shem 26. The number echoes through Scripture and tradition: the seventy souls of Jacob's house (Genesis 46:27; Deuteronomy 32:8), and the seventy bulls of Sukkot, offered for the nations of the world (Numbers 29; Sukkah 55b).

Many names are peoples (Ludim, the Jebusite) or places (Sidon, Hazarmaveth) rather than individuals: a map of the known world drawn as a family. The chapter gives Japheth first and Shem last, because Shem's line leads on to Abraham.
countNote: Filled dots are the seventy. Nimrod (an individual) and the Philistines ("from whom… came") are counted differently by different readers; one of the two makes up Ham's thirty.
sources: Hebrew names: Miqra according to the Masorah. Jewish tradition: Josephus, Antiquities 1.122–147; Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 10a; Genesis Rabbah 37; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan; Rashi on Genesis 10. Scholarly identifications summarise the views found in the standard commentaries and reference works (e.g. Sarna, JPS Torah Commentary: Genesis; Wenham, Genesis 1–15; Westermann, Genesis 1–11; Anchor Bible Dictionary). Certainty labels are our own summary. Parallel list: 1 Chronicles 1:4–27.

people.trad: The rabbis teach that the seven commandments given to Noah and his sons (the Noahide laws) bind all the nations listed here (Sanhedrin 56a).
people.sch: The chapter is a toledot ("these are the generations"), one of the headings that structure Genesis.
people.note: Seventy names descend from his three sons. Jewish tradition reads them as the seventy nations of the world.

people.g: peoples of the north and the coastlands
people.trad: Noah's blessing, "May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem" (9:27), was read by the sages to mean that the beauty of Japheth, the Greek language, may dwell in the tents of Shem; so the Torah may be written in Greek (Megillah 9b).
people.sch: His line covers Anatolia, the Aegean, the Caucasus and Iran: the northern and western edge of the world known to Israel.
people.note: His line is given first and most briefly; the chapter moves from the far peoples to the near ones, ending with Shem.

people.trad: Josephus: the Galatians, once called Gomerites (Ant. 1.123). Talmud: "Germamya" (Yoma 10a).
people.sch: The Cimmerians (Akkadian Gimirrai), horse-riding people from north of the Black Sea who swept into Anatolia in the 8th–7th centuries BC. Ezekiel 38:6 places Gomer among the northern allies of Gog.

people.trad: In medieval Hebrew Ashkenaz became the name for the Germanic lands (hence "Ashkenazi" Jews). Josephus: the Rheginians (Ant. 1.126).
people.sch: Most likely the Scythians (Assyrian Ashkuza). Jeremiah 51:27 calls the kingdoms "Ararat, Minni and Ashkenaz" to war against Babylon, which fits the region of Lake Urmia.

people.trad: Josephus: the Paphlagonians, on the south coast of the Black Sea (Ant. 1.126).
people.sch: Not identified. 1 Chronicles 1:6 reads Diphath, a common d/r confusion in Hebrew script.

people.trad: Josephus: the Phrygians (Ant. 1.126). In the tenth-century Khazar correspondence the Khazar king traces his people to Togarmah, and medieval Jewish writers used the name for the Turkic peoples. Armenian tradition also claims him as ancestor.
people.sch: Hittite and Assyrian Tegarama, a city and district of eastern Anatolia near the upper Euphrates (around modern Gürün). Ezekiel 27:14 has Beth-togarmah trading horses and mules with Tyre.

people.trad: Josephus: the Scythians (Ant. 1.123). Talmud: "Kandiya" (Yoma 10a). Through Ezekiel 38–39, "Gog of the land of Magog" became in Jewish and Christian tradition the name for the final enemy of God's people.
people.sch: Not securely identified. Often linked with the Scythians or with Lydia (Gyges, Assyrian Gugu); "Magog" may mean "land of Gog."

people.trad: Josephus: the Medes (Ant. 1.124). Talmud: Macedonia (Yoma 10a).
people.sch: The Medes of north-western Iran; Madai is the ordinary Hebrew name for Media (2 Kgs 17:6; Esther 1:3; Daniel 5:28).

people.trad: Josephus: Ionia and all the Greeks (Ant. 1.124). Talmud: "in its plain sense," Greece (Yoma 10a). Yavan remains the Hebrew name for Greece; in Daniel 8:21 and the Hanukkah story Yavan is the Hellenistic kingdom.
people.sch: The Ionians, the Greeks of the west coast of Anatolia and the islands (Assyrian Yamnaya); the name later stood for all Greeks.

people.trad: Josephus: the Aeolians (Ant. 1.127).
people.sch: Probably Alashiya, the Bronze Age name for Cyprus or part of it, known from the Amarna letters and Ugarit. Ezekiel 27:7 speaks of purple dye "from the coasts of Elishah."

people.trad: Josephus: Tarsus in Cilicia (Ant. 1.127). The Targum of the prophets often renders Tarshish as "the sea" or Africa.
people.sch: A distant western port reached by "ships of Tarshish" (Jonah 1:3; 1 Kgs 10:22). Proposals: Tartessos in southern Spain, Sardinia (the Nora stone names trshsh), or Tarsus. The phrase "ships of Tarshish" came to mean large ocean-going ships.

people.trad: Josephus: Cyprus, named from the city of Kition (Ant. 1.128). Later Jewish usage widened Kittim to Greeks (1 Maccabees 1:1, of Alexander) and Romans (Daniel 11:30; the Dead Sea Scrolls).
people.sch: Kition (modern Larnaca) on Cyprus, a Phoenician port; by extension the people of Cyprus and the eastern Mediterranean islands.

people.trad: The traditional Hebrew text reads Dodanim; 1 Chronicles 1:7, the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint read Rodanim.
people.sch: With the reading Rodanim, most scholars identify the people of Rhodes. With Dodanim, some suggest the Dardanians of north-west Anatolia.
people.note: The BSB follows the Rodanim reading ("Rodanites"); see its footnote at 10:4.

people.trad: Josephus: the Iberians of the Caucasus (Ant. 1.124). Talmud: "Beit Unaiki," probably Bithynia (Yoma 10a).
people.sch: Tabal, a kingdom in central and south-eastern Anatolia in Assyrian records. Almost always paired with Meshech (Ezekiel 27:13; 38:2).

people.trad: Josephus: the Cappadocians, whose city was Mazaca (Ant. 1.125). Talmud: Mysia (Yoma 10a).
people.sch: The Mushki of Assyrian texts, a people of central Anatolia linked with the Phrygians (King Mita of Mushki, the Midas of Greek legend).

people.trad: Josephus: the Thracians (Ant. 1.125). Talmud: Rav Yosef taught that Tiras is Persia; another view, "Beit Teraiki," Thrace (Yoma 10a).
people.sch: Often linked with the Tursha, one of the Sea Peoples in Egyptian texts, and so perhaps with the Tyrsenians (Etruscans) of Greek writers.

people.trad: Jewish tradition connects Ham with the incident of 9:20–27, where the curse falls on his son Canaan rather than on Ham himself (Rashi on 9:25).
people.sch: His line covers Africa (Cush, Egypt, Libya), southern Arabia and the land of Canaan: peoples tied to Egypt by geography and politics rather than by language (Canaanite is a Semitic tongue).
people.note: "Land of Ham" is a poetic name for Egypt (Psalm 105:23).

people.trad: Josephus: the Ethiopians, still called Cushites (Ant. 1.131).
people.sch: Kush, the kingdom south of Egypt on the Nile, in today's Sudan (Egyptian Kash). Cush's sons point to the Red Sea coasts of Africa and Arabia.
people.note: The Cush who fathers Nimrod (10:8) may be a different, Mesopotamian Cush, perhaps the Kassites.

people.trad: Josephus: the Sabaeans (Ant. 1.134).
people.sch: An African people named with Egypt and Cush (Isaiah 43:3; 45:14), perhaps on the African Red Sea coast; distinct in Hebrew spelling from Sheba.

people.trad: Josephus: the Getuli of north-west Africa (Ant. 1.134).
people.sch: A region of Arabia; Genesis 25:18 sets the Ishmaelites "from Havilah to Shur." Havilah appears again among Joktan's sons (10:29): a people of the Red Sea trade with both African and Arabian ties.

people.trad: Josephus: the Astaborans (Ant. 1.134). Talmud: "inner Sakistan" (Yoma 10a).
people.sch: Perhaps Shabwa, the ancient capital of Hadramawt in southern Arabia.

people.trad: Josephus: the Ragmeans (Ant. 1.135).
people.sch: Traders with Tyre together with Sheba (Ezekiel 27:22); perhaps Rgmt of the Sabaean inscriptions, near Najran.

people.trad: The Queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon (1 Kgs 10) made Sheba proverbial for wealth and wisdom.
people.sch: Saba, the incense kingdom of Yemen (capital Marib). Sheba appears three times in Genesis: here, among Joktan's sons (10:28), and with Dedan among Abraham's descendants by Keturah (25:3).
people.note: Such repetitions show that the chapter maps peoples by their connections (trade, region, alliance) as much as by descent.

people.trad: Josephus, reading a different text, names the Judadeans of western Ethiopia (Ant. 1.135).
people.sch: The oasis of Dedan, modern al-'Ula in north-west Saudi Arabia, a caravan city known from its own inscriptions (Ezekiel 27:20; Jeremiah 25:23).

people.trad: Josephus: the Sabactens (Ant. 1.135). Talmud: "outer Sakistan" (Yoma 10a).
people.sch: Not identified.

people.trad: The sages read his name from marad, "to rebel." Rashi: "He ensnared the minds of people by his words, misleading them to rebel against the Omnipresent" (on 10:9, from Genesis Rabbah 37:2). Josephus makes him the instigator of the Tower of Babel (Ant. 1.113–114), and the midrash sets him against Abraham (Genesis Rabbah 38:13).
people.sch: No certain identification. Proposals include Ninurta, the Mesopotamian god of war and hunting, and kings such as Sargon of Akkad or Tukulti-Ninurta I. Micah 5:6 calls Assyria "the land of Nimrod."
people.note: His cities (10:10–12): Babylon; Erech (Uruk); Accad (Agade); Calneh (unknown); Nineveh; Rehoboth-Ir; Calah (Nimrud); Resen. An individual rather than a people, so he is usually left out of the seventy.

people.trad: Josephus: the Egyptians, who call their land Mestre (Ant. 1.132). The dual ending is traditionally explained as the "two Egypts," Upper and Lower.
people.sch: The ordinary Hebrew name of Egypt. His "sons" are peoples within and around Egypt, all given in plural form.

people.trad: Josephus lists the name without identifying it (Ant. 1.137).
people.sch: Unclear. Some read Lubim (Libyans); others think of Lydian mercenaries serving in Egypt (Jeremiah 46:9 has Lud with Cush and Put). Distinct from Shem's son Lud (10:22).

people.trad: Josephus lists the name without identifying it (Ant. 1.137).
people.sch: Not identified; perhaps the people of the Kharga oasis in Egypt's western desert.

people.trad: Josephus: they settled Libya (Ant. 1.137).
people.sch: Usually taken as the Lubim, the Libyans west of Egypt (2 Chronicles 12:3; Nahum 3:9).

people.trad: Josephus lists the name without identifying it (Ant. 1.137).
people.sch: Perhaps from Egyptian p3-t3-mḥw, "the northland," the Nile Delta.

people.trad: Josephus lists the name without identifying it (Ant. 1.137).
people.sch: People of Pathros, Egyptian p3-t3-rsy, "the southland": Upper Egypt (Isaiah 11:11; Jeremiah 44:1).

people.trad: Josephus lists the name without identifying it (Ant. 1.137).
people.sch: Not identified.

people.trad: Josephus: the Philistines, after whom the Greeks call part of the land Palestine (Ant. 1.136).
people.sch: One of the Sea Peoples (Egyptian Peleset) who settled the southern coast around 1175 BC; their pottery and customs are Aegean. Amos 9:7 and Jeremiah 47:4 bring them from Caphtor, so some scholars think the clause "from whom the Philistines came" belongs after the Caphtorim.
people.note: Introduced as "came from," not as a son, so they are sometimes left out of the seventy and sometimes counted in Nimrod's place.

people.trad: Targum Pseudo-Jonathan renders the name "Kappadokians."
people.sch: Caphtor is Crete (Egyptian Keftiu, Akkadian Kaptara) and the Aegean world (Deuteronomy 2:23; Amos 9:7).

people.trad: Josephus: the Libyans, called Phutites, after a river in Mauretania (Ant. 1.132–133).
people.sch: Libya (Old Persian Putaya); some suggest Punt on the Red Sea. Put supplies soldiers to Egypt and Tyre (Jeremiah 46:9; Ezekiel 27:10).

people.trad: Josephus: the land later called Judea (Ant. 1.134). The sages read Canaan's listing among Ham's sons together with the curse of 9:25.
people.sch: The peoples of the coast and hills between Gaza and Phoenicia. Linguistically Canaanite is Semitic, close to Hebrew; Canaan is placed with Egypt because the land was long under Egyptian rule.
people.note: His eleven "sons" include a city (Sidon) and ten peoples in the singular gentilic form ("the Jebusite").

people.trad: Josephus: the city of Sidon, called by the Greeks Sidon too (Ant. 1.138).
people.sch: Sidon (Saida, Lebanon), one of the oldest Phoenician cities; "firstborn" reflects its seniority. "Sidonians" can stand for all Phoenicians (1 Kgs 16:31).

people.trad: Abraham buys the cave of Machpelah from "the sons of Heth" at Hebron (Genesis 23).
people.sch: The biblical Hittites of the hill country may be a local people with no direct link to the Hittite empire of Anatolia; others connect them with the Neo-Hittite kingdoms of Syria. Debated.
people.note: The Hebrew text has "Heth"; the BSB renders it "the Hittites."

people.trad: The Jebusites held Jerusalem until David took it (2 Samuel 5:6–9); David bought the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, the site of the Temple (2 Samuel 24:18–25).
people.sch: The people of Jebus, the name the Bible gives Jerusalem before David (Judges 19:10).

people.trad: "The iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete" (Genesis 15:16) became a rabbinic byword for God's patience with the nations.
people.sch: The Amurru, "westerners," a West-Semitic people well known in Mesopotamian sources (Hammurabi's dynasty was Amorite). In the Bible often the hill-country population of Canaan and Transjordan.

people.trad: The Jerusalem Talmud teaches that the Girgashites left the land before Israel entered and were given a land in Africa (Shevi'it 6:1).
people.sch: Not identified. grgš occurs as a name at Ugarit; some link the Karkisha of Hittite and Egyptian texts.

people.trad: The Gibeonites who deceived Joshua were Hivites (Joshua 9:7), as were the people of Shechem (Genesis 34:2).
people.sch: Found at Shechem, Gibeon and below Mount Hermon (Joshua 11:3). Some scholars identify them with the Hurrians.

people.trad: Josephus: Arce in Lebanon (Ant. 1.138).
people.sch: Arqa (Tell Arqa), north-east of Tripoli in Lebanon, a city known from the Amarna letters.

people.trad: Josephus lists them among the peoples whose cities were destroyed (Ant. 1.139).
people.sch: Perhaps Siyannu near Ugarit, or a town near Arqa; named with other cities of the northern coast.

people.trad: Josephus: the island of Aradus (Ant. 1.138).
people.sch: Arwad, the island city off the Syrian coast; its sailors served Tyre (Ezekiel 27:8, 11).

people.trad: Josephus lists them among the peoples whose cities were destroyed (Ant. 1.139).
people.sch: Sumur, probably Tell Kazel near the Syrian coast, prominent in the Amarna letters.

people.trad: Josephus: Amathe, renamed Epiphania by the Macedonians (Ant. 1.138).
people.sch: Hamath (Hama) on the Orontes in Syria; "Lebo-hamath" marks Israel's ideal northern border (Numbers 34:8).

people.trad: The sages identify Shem with Melchizedek, king of Salem (Nedarim 32b; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on 14:18). Tradition tells of the study house of Shem and Eber, where Rebekah went to inquire of the LORD and Jacob studied (Rashi on 25:22; Megillah 17a).
people.sch: His line covers Mesopotamia, Syria and Arabia. "Semitic," a modern term for the language family, is taken from his name, though the lists do not follow language strictly (Elam was not Semitic-speaking).
people.note: His line comes last because it leads on to Abraham (11:10–26). "Father of all the children of Eber" (10:21) points ahead to the Hebrews.

people.trad: Josephus: the Elamites, ancestors of the Persians (Ant. 1.143).
people.sch: Elam, the kingdom of south-western Iran with its capital at Susa (Daniel 8:2). Its language is not Semitic; it is placed here by geography.

people.trad: Rashi on 10:11: "As soon as Asshur saw that his sons listened to Nimrod, rebelling against the Omnipresent by building the Tower, he went forth out of their midst" (from Genesis Rabbah 37:4). Josephus: the Assyrians, whose city was Nineveh (Ant. 1.143).
people.sch: Assyria and its first capital Ashur on the Tigris.

people.trad: Josephus: the Chaldeans (Ant. 1.143–144).
people.sch: Unexplained. The ending -kshad may contain Kasdim, the Chaldeans; some suggest Arrapha (near Kirkuk).
people.note: The Septuagint adds Cainan as his son (followed in Luke 3:36).

people.trad: Listed in the line from Shem to Abraham (11:12–15).
people.sch: No people of this name is known; he is a link in the chosen line.
people.note: The Septuagint and Luke 3:35–36 put Cainan between Arphaxad and Shelah (BSB footnote at 10:24).

people.trad: The midrash plays on ever, "the other side": "the whole world stood on one side and Abraham on the other" (Genesis Rabbah 42:8, on "Abram the Hebrew," 14:13). Rashi on 10:25: Eber was a prophet, for he named his son after the division that was coming.
people.sch: The eponym of the Hebrews (ivri). Shem is called "father of all the children of Eber" (10:21), a wider group than Israel alone.

people.trad: Rashi: the earth was "divided" when "the languages became confounded and they were scattered abroad from the plain of Shinar" (on 10:25), the dispersion of Babel (11:1–9).
people.sch: The name means "division"; Akkadian palgu is an irrigation canal, so some see a memory of the dividing of the land by canals.
people.note: His line continues in 11:18–26 to Terah and Abram.

people.trad: Rashi: "He was so called ('the little one') because he was so humble and thought little of himself," and so merited to found all these families (on 10:25). Arab genealogy traces the southern Arabs to Qahtan, usually equated with Joktan.
people.sch: Father of thirteen peoples of southern Arabia; several of their names are known places in Yemen and Hadramawt.

people.trad: Targum Pseudo-Jonathan: "who measured the earth with lines."
people.sch: Not identified; perhaps "God is friend" or "the beloved."

people.trad: Targum Pseudo-Jonathan: "who drew out the waters of rivers."
people.sch: Perhaps the Yemeni tribe or district of Salif.

people.trad: The name reads in Hebrew as "court of death."
people.sch: Hadramawt, the incense region of southern Yemen; the name is the same word.

people.trad: The name means "moon."
people.sch: Not identified.

people.trad: Listed without comment in the rabbinic sources.
people.sch: Not identified.

people.trad: Arab and Jewish tradition give Azal as the old name of Sanaa, the capital of Yemen.
people.sch: Possibly Sanaa; Ezekiel 27:19 may name Uzal among the traders of Tyre.

people.trad: The name means "date palm."
people.sch: Not identified; probably an oasis.

people.trad: 1 Chronicles 1:22 reads Ebal.
people.sch: Not identified.

people.trad: The name means "my father is God" or similar.
people.sch: Not identified; the name has a South Arabian form.

people.trad: See Sheba son of Raamah (10:7).
people.sch: Saba in Yemen. The same people is listed under both Cush and Joktan, reflecting its African and Arabian ties.

people.trad: "Gold of Ophir" became proverbial (Psalm 45:9; Job 28:16).
people.sch: Solomon's ships brought gold from Ophir (1 Kgs 9:28). Location debated: southern Arabia, the Horn of Africa, or India. An ostracon from Tell Qasile (8th century BC) reads "gold of Ophir to Beth-horon."

people.trad: See Havilah son of Cush (10:7).
people.sch: A region of Arabia, listed under both Cush and Joktan.

people.trad: Listed without comment in the rabbinic sources.
people.sch: Not identified; distinct from Jobab king of Edom (Genesis 36:33).

people.trad: Josephus: the Lydians of western Anatolia (Ant. 1.144).
people.sch: Usually Lydia (Assyrian Luddu), though Lydia lies far from the other sons of Shem; perhaps placed here for political reasons. Distinct from the Ludim of Egypt (10:13).

people.trad: Josephus: the Arameans, whom the Greeks call Syrians (Ant. 1.144). Israel's ancestors are remembered as Arameans: "A wandering Aramean was my father" (Deuteronomy 26:5), recited at the Passover Seder.
people.sch: The Arameans of Syria and upper Mesopotamia, whose language, Aramaic, became the common tongue of the Near East and of parts of Daniel, Ezra and the Talmud.

people.trad: Josephus: founder of Trachonitis and Damascus (Ant. 1.145). Job lived "in the land of Uz" (Job 1:1).
people.sch: Location debated: the Hauran south of Damascus, or the borders of Edom (Lamentations 4:21).

people.trad: Josephus: Armenia (Ant. 1.145).
people.sch: Not identified.

people.trad: Josephus: the Bactrians (Ant. 1.145).
people.sch: Not identified.

people.trad: Josephus: the Mesaneans at Charax Spasinu (Ant. 1.145). 1 Chronicles 1:17 reads Meshech.
people.sch: Perhaps Mount Masius (Tur Abdin) in northern Mesopotamia; not certain.
